intro: Slack for documentary filmmakers on Mac is the chat layer for a production. Set it up with one channel per stage, threads for every decision, and a plan that keeps your history long enough. This guide covers channels, the free plan limits, Clips, Workflow Builder, and where Lazur fits while you work.
tldr: Give each production stage its own channel, such as #edit-rough-cut or #color, and keep every decision in a thread.
The free plan keeps 90 days of searchable history and allows only one-to-one huddles. Most production teams need a paid plan.
Clips record audio or video up to 5 minutes from the message field, and video clips get closed captions.
Workflow Builder needs a paid plan, except for Frontline Members. Lazur guides you through steps but does not click for you.

blocks.text: How to set up Slack for a documentary production on Mac

Start with one workspace for each production, not one big workspace for everything. If you work on several films, keep them apart. Musicbed's filmmakers describe the same pattern: channels per department or stage, plus a temporary separate workspace for clients. That split keeps the editor's notes away from the client's approval thread.

Name channels by stage. A prefix makes the sidebar easy to scan and search easy to filter. A channel called #general tells you nothing once the edit is underway. A channel called #edit-rough-cut tells you where to look.

rows: Cut notes, timecodes, picture lock dates
Grade references, LUT files, review links
Dialogue cleanup notes, music cue list
Edit changes that are not final
blocks.caption: A starting set of channels for one documentary. Rename them to match your stages.

blocks.text: Keep one channel for announcements. Post the screening date, the drive handover, and the lock date there, and nothing else. A new crew member should be able to scroll it in ten seconds. If it fills with cut debate, move that debate into #edit-rough-cut.

Watch for channels that outlive their stage. Once a film locks picture, #edit-rough-cut turns into a graveyard of old timecodes. Archive it, or rename it with the lock date, so the next search does not return last year's cut notes first.
Keep Slack quiet with channel rules and notifications

A filmmaker writing on Storyflow's blog puts it bluntly. Storyflow sells its own film collaboration tool, and the author says so. Slack, the author says, gets noisy fast when channels have no rules. The same author says it is a poor place for creative or production work. The noise is fixable. The creative work belongs in your editing software, not in chat.
Four rules cut most of the noise.

items: Put each decision in a thread under the message it answers. The reasoning stays attached to the decision.
Write timecodes in every note, such as 01:04:22, not only the scene name. The editor can find the moment in seconds.
Move arguments to a call. Post the outcome in the channel, in one line.
Mute channels you read on your own time. Keep the cut and color channels loud during delivery week.

blocks.text: Pause alerts for focused work instead of muting the whole app. You can set a pause from the profile menu, or set a schedule. The [pause notifications guide](/how-to/pause-notifications-in-slack) walks through each option.

blocks.title: Mute channels, not Slack
blocks.text: Muting all of Slack hides the message that matters, like a client note that arrives late in the afternoon. Mute the channels that do not need you, and keep the active ones on. The [mute a channel guide](/how-to/mute-a-channel-in-slack) shows the steps.
Free plan limits: history, huddles and what the upgrade buys

The free plan works for a short test. It is a weak base for a film that runs through a long edit and a festival run. Slack's pricing page says Free keeps messages searchable for 90 days. You can extend that to 12 months by upgrading, and paid plans keep unlimited history.

blocks.caption: Based on Slack's pricing page. Confirm current terms before you buy.

blocks.text: Huddles are the other gap. Free workspaces allow only one-to-one huddles. A call with the editor, the colorist and the producer needs a group huddle. Pro, Business+ and Enterprise+ include them. If the crew talks every day, that gap is the reason to upgrade.

Decide on history before the work gets heavy. Once a message ages out of the free window, search cannot find it. Check the age of your oldest decision today. If it is close to 90 days old, upgrade before you lose it.
Search threads and find a decision from last month

Most of your work in Slack is looking things up. Use the search bar at the top of the window. Type a word unique to the decision, such as a clip name or a lab roll number. Then filter by channel or person. Open the thread, because the answer often sits in a reply.

items: Search by a rare word, not by cut. Every channel uses that word, so the results flood the screen.
Filter by channel first when you know the stage. The results shrink fast.
Search the timecode format you always use, such as 01:04, to find notes about one moment.
Read the whole thread. A reply on Tuesday can overturn the message from Monday.

blocks.text: For search inside one conversation, follow the [search inside a conversation guide](/how-to/search-inside-a-conversation-in-slack). The [search messages guide](/how-to/search-messages-in-slack) covers the full results page.
Clips: short audio and video notes instead of long calls

Clips are easy to overlook. You can record audio or video straight from the message field, with no separate app. Slack allows clips up to five minutes on every plan, and video clips get closed captions. Check the captions before you rely on them for a note that names a person or a place.

items: Click into the message field in a channel or thread.
Click the camera icon for video, or the microphone icon for audio.
Click Record, then talk through the note. Say the timecode out loud.
Click the check mark to stop, then send the clip.

blocks.text: Clips suit notes that need tone. A producer's reaction to a rough cut sounds different from a written line. A colorist can hear the hesitation. Record a short clip for those notes, then write the decision in text for the record.

blocks.title: A clip is not an approval
blocks.text: Clips are easy to send and easy to bury. Write the final decision in the thread, with the cut version. A clip alone does not show what was approved.
Mac permissions for huddles, camera and screen share

Huddles and screen share fail on Mac more often than they should. macOS blocks the app until you allow it. Slack's help article names three permissions: Microphone and Camera for huddles, and Screen Recording for screen sharing. The article uses older menu names, so look for the same items in the current settings.

items: Quit Slack with ⌘Q.
Go to System Settings > Privacy & Security.
Open Microphone and turn on Slack. Do the same under Camera. For sharing, find the Screen Recording entry and turn on Slack. On newer macOS versions it may read Screen & System Audio Recording.
Reopen Slack and start the huddle again.

blocks.title: Share one window, not the screen
blocks.text: Share a single window during a call. Close private messages, password managers and personal mail first. Everything visible on the shared screen goes to the call.
Workflow Builder for posts, reminders and cut alerts

Workflow Builder runs simple automations inside Slack. Anyone on a paid plan can build workflows, except Frontline Members. Owners or admins can restrict who builds them. The free plan does not include it.

items: Click Agents & tools in the sidebar. If you do not see it, open the Tools tab under More.
Under Workflows, click New, then choose Build Workflow.
Pick a start trigger, then add each step.
Test in a private channel before you touch a production channel.

blocks.text: Start triggers include a shared link, a webhook, a schedule, a list item update, a message being posted, a person joining a channel, and an emoji reaction. Two of them fit production work well. A schedule can post a weekly status line. An emoji reaction can start a flow when an editor marks a cut as ready.
Worked example: a cut-ready alert

items: Trigger: an emoji reaction on the cut post in #edit-rough-cut. Use a checkmark, so the editor knows the rule.
Step: post the cut link and version number in #color.
Step: post a reminder in #sound-mix with the reel length.
Keep the client step manual. An automated post to a client channel is hard to take back.

blocks.text: Run a test with a dummy message before the real cut. A workflow that posts the wrong link to the client is a bad morning. Watch the first live run on the same day, not the next.
Where Lazur helps while you work in Slack

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Ask where a channel is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it on your screen.

Ask how to do something and Lazur guides you one click at a time. It waits for each click. That helps when a Slack menu has moved since the last time you used it. You still press every button. Lazur does not click, edit files or operate other apps for you.

Hold fn to dictate. Clean, formatted text appears at the cursor in any app, so you can talk a reply into the message field. Add snippets for things you type every day, such as the screening address. Add film terms to your personal dictionary, including lab names, lens models and festival names.

Lazur is most useful for the small questions. Where is the grade reference? What did the producer say about the cut length? Those questions cost a few minutes each in a busy channel. Asking out loud keeps your hands on the timeline.
Client access and approvals without leaking the edit

Keep client access in a separate space, so the client never sees internal debate. Musicbed's filmmakers describe the same setup, with clients in a temporary separate workspace. Post only approved links to the client side. Never paste an internal thread into a client channel to explain a decision.

A simple approval trail helps you later. Post the cut link, the version name and the date in the client channel. Ask the client to reply in the same thread. When a note comes back months later, you can point to the thread.
Mistakes that cost filmmakers time in Slack

items: Sending a client a link from an internal channel. Check the channel name before you paste.
Keeping decisions in direct messages. The team cannot search them, and neither can you after a handover.
Letting the free history window pass. Once a message ages out, search cannot find it.
Muting everything during delivery week. Mute the noise, and keep the cut and color channels on.
Sharing the full screen in a huddle. Share one window instead.

blocks.text: Most of these mistakes are habits, not settings. Fix the habit first. The settings only help once the habit is clear.
What a small documentary team pays for Slack

Slack's pricing page lists Pro at $8.75 per user per month billed monthly, or $7.25 per user per month billed annually. Business+ is $18 monthly or $15 annually. Check the pricing page before you commit, because prices change.
Take a team of four on Pro. Billed annually, four seats at $7.25 come to $29 a month. Billed monthly, four seats at $8.75 come to $35 a month. The annual plan saves $6 a month for that team.
The monthly promotion of 50% off for three months does not apply to annual plans. Read the terms before you count on it. Budget the full annual rate for a film that runs for a long time.
Why Slack gets harder to manage as the crew grows
Slack's Workforce Index, from June 2024, found that 75% of knowledge workers use more apps than they did five years earlier. More apps mean more places for a note to go missing.

Slack's own State of Work survey, of about 17,000 knowledge workers, reports that 68% spend at least 30 minutes a day switching between tools. The article does not say which year the survey covers, so treat it as a rough signal.
Slack is a vendor, so read these numbers with that in mind. Use them to decide where your team's attention goes. Do not treat them as proof that a tool fixes the problem.
Keyboard shortcuts for Slack on Mac

items: ⌘K opens the quick switcher. Type a channel or a person's name, then press Return.
⇧ Return starts a new line in the message field without sending it.

blocks.text: For the full list, read the [keyboard shortcuts guide](/how-to/show-the-keyboard-shortcuts-list-in-slack). Shortcuts stick when you use them on the same tasks each day, such as jumping between the cut and color channels.
First week checklist for a new production workspace

items: Create one channel per stage, plus one announcements channel and one client channel.
Check your history plan before the first shoot, and upgrade if the film is long.
Agree on the clip habit: record notes as clips, and write decisions in threads.
Run a test huddle with the editor, and fix any Mac permission before the real call.
Build one workflow and test it in a private channel.

blocks.text: If a menu does not match these steps, ask Lazur to walk you through it. It stays one click at a time, and you stay in control of the Mac. You can [get Lazur for Mac here](/download).

faq.question: Is Slack for documentary filmmakers on Mac free to use?
faq.answer: Slack has a Free plan. It keeps messages searchable for 90 days, and it allows only one-to-one huddles. Paid plans keep unlimited history and include group huddles. Check Slack's pricing page for current terms.

faq.question: How long can a Slack clip be?
faq.answer: Slack's help article says audio and video clips can run up to five minutes. Clips work on all plans. Video clips get closed captions. Record the clip from the camera or microphone icon in the message field.

faq.question: Can clients join the production Slack?
faq.answer: Musicbed describes adding clients to a temporary separate workspace. Keep the internal crew workspace separate from client approvals. Check Slack's help center for the current guest rules on your plan.

faq.question: Why won't huddles or screen share work on my Mac?
faq.answer: Most often, macOS has not allowed Slack to use the microphone, camera or screen. Go to System Settings > Privacy & Security, and turn on Slack for each item. Quit Slack and reopen it before you start the huddle again.

faq.question: Does Workflow Builder work on the free plan?
faq.answer: No. Anyone on a paid plan can create workflows, except Frontline Members. Owners or admins can restrict who builds them. Open the Build a workflow help article on Slack's site for the current steps.

faq.question: Can Lazur click buttons in Slack for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons or operate other apps. It points, explains, answers out loud, types text, and guides you one click at a time. You still press every button yourself.

faq.question: Does Lazur listen to my Slack messages all the time?
faq.answer: No. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut, which is Option and Command. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer and are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models.

faq.question: Does Lazur work inside Slack like a plugin?
faq.answer: No. Lazur is not a plugin or add-in for any app, and that includes Slack. It is a voice assistant for the Mac that sits beside the apps you already use. It points, explains, answers out loud and types text.

faq.question: Does Lazur work on Windows for Slack?
faq.answer: Lazur runs on macOS, on both Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, but it is not available yet.
